[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Freud's theory of a psychoanalytic psychology portrays the mind as a closed intrapsychic system. However, the description of the therapeutic relationship, the source of the empirical data for the theory, emphasized interaction and intersubjectivity. Neither Freud nor the analysts that followed him have ever adequately been able to bridge the intrapsychic and interactional realms.

Gill and the authors of the papers in this issue continue to create a reconciliation of the intrapsychic and interactional realms. All the contributors believe that the difference between Gill and themselves is one of degree of emphasis between intrapsychic, interaction, and intersubjective. But Gill, in his bold response, claims that his position is not based upon differences in emphasis. Contrarily, he is advocating a different definition of transference—a definition that includes a social perspective incompatible with a definition of transference that does not account for the actual interactional component of the relationship. Thus Gill continues to approach a new paradigm for psychoanalysis wherein the central motivational unit is interaction not drive discharge. Our issue ends with no concensus, but given the stimulus provided by Gill and the essayists, we can be certain that the immediate future of psychoanalysis will be rich in growth and creativity.

Epilogue

Warren Poland Issue Editor and René Major Issue Editor

René Major

René Major  

The meetings of the first Franco-American Encounter in Paris in 1983 started with possible confusion arising from the discomfort of confronting one's usual vantage point with strange ways of approaching analytic questions. Despite the presence of both subtle and substantial differences in basic conceptualizations, participants from each side of the Atlantic came to recognize a commonality of clinical and theoretical concerns. The need to stretch beyond oneself to understand the ideas of foreign colleagues is an exercise too easily avoided.

The French contributors to this volume have addressed questions of analytic theory and practice already under scrutiny by Americans. Yet the effort to follow a different turn of mind, a strange way of thought or fashion of speech, is repaid by more than new insights into ideas of others; it also brings a fresh grasp of one's own thinking, which at times may be left too long unquestioned.

The authors included in this issue have struggled with understanding the nature of transference, of relations of love and hate, of the implications of otherness; the role of words and signifiers in analysis; the vicissitudes of sexuality and aggression; the manifestations of oedipal subtleties in the analytic process. The interests of American psychoanalysts are the same.

Attention to the French authors adds to our knowledge their advances. But just as valuable is the way they enable us to step back from our own frames of reference and to view our own attitudes in a new light.

[[RunningHead]]

Analysis of the Transference: Implications for Theory and Research

Alan Skolnikoff MD

Alan Skolnikoff

205 Edgewood Avenue
San Francisco, California 94117

Alan Skolnikoff  

In this review, after commenting on my agreements and disagreements with Gill and Hoffman's presentations, I wish to outline some of the implications that this excellent work has for the theory of technique and the practice of psychoanalysis. What is most interesting in this presentation is that the authors provide us, in Volume II (Gill & Hoffman, 1982), with verbatim transcripts. Not only do they demonstrate what therapists who are proponents of the centrality of transference do in analytic or therapy hours, but they also contrast this material with hours representative of therapists who do not necessarily espouse this principle. I have elsewhere, (1984) agreed with Gill's (1982) statements that (1) priority should be given to the analysis of resistance to the awareness of the transference, and (2) that instead of resolving the transference by relating it to contemporary, genetic, or extratransference material, further work should be done to clarifying it within the analytic situation. This would include aspects of the transference not yet in awareness and can be accomplished by further assessing features of the analytic situation that might conceal transference and countertransference attitudes. Some writers (Stone, 1981) think that the emphasis on the here-and-now runs the risk of devaluating the importance of the past, either in pathogenesis or in the analytic process.

Dr. Skolnikoff is Associate Clinical Professor, University of California, San Francisco Department of Psychiatry; he is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute.

Prologue

Donald Silver MD

Donald Silver

Donald Silver  

All exercises in the realm of psychoanalytic biography can have one of two purposes. They may either focus on creative individuals in order to illuminate the creative process, or they may focus on genetic, dynamic, and contextual factors in order to facilitate comprehension of particular creative individuals. In the most outstanding works of this genre, these two orientations are combined in reciprocally illuminating ways. The psychoanalytic biographer's own creative amalgamation of nature and nurture, his willingness to construe creativity as the outcome of an interaction between innate predisposition and historical circumstances, is in some ways analogous to the psychoanalyst's clinical work. It is the psychoanalytic biographer's creative achievement, we might say, to keep us “on the ground” in ascertaining the endlessly complex relationship between certain general constituents of the creative process and the peculiarities of creative individuals in whom the process is exemplified.

These provisos are particularly germane in approaching Goethe, whose profound poetic sensibilities are complemented by the profoundly biographical import of his poetic creations. Goethe's immense stature in the Western literary tradition is sufficient reason to make him the subject of an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry. For psychoanalysts, Goethe holds special appeal. Freud, as Leon Wurmser points out in the introductory chapter, was not only steeped in a Goethean heritage, but undertook to address in psychoanalytic therapy some of the very questions that preoccupied Goethe. Friederike Brion and the Origins of Faust

Donald Silver MD

Donald Silver

26111 14 Mile Road
Franklin, Michigan 48025

Donald Silver  

Among topics of continuing interest to Goethe scholars, the complicated chronology of the writing of Faust occupies a special place. We know that the poet first set down Faust in rough outline form in the winter of 1771-1772 when he was 22-23 years old. Although he modified it slightly before moving to Weimar in 1775, he did not seriously pursue the project further until his return from Italy in 1790. It was at this time that he converted the play from prose to poetry and published Part I without the epilogue. The Goethe who published Part I of Faust in 1790 at the age of 40 was far from the brash youth who had set down his ideas about Faust in the original manuscript of 1771. During this crucial 20-year period Goethe had lost his beloved sister, Cornelia; he had established an intense relationship with Frau Charlotte von Stein, a married woman seven years older than he was and evidently an object of platonic love. By 1790, moreover, he had taken a mistress while traveling in Italy and presumably achieved potency, for he returned from the prolonged holiday a changed man. It was shortly thereafter that he began the affair with Christiane that culminated in his marriage to her in 1806.

I am concerned here with the young Goethe and the circumstances leading to his writing of the Urfaust. I agree with Eissler (1963)

Dr. Silver is a Lecturer at Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Donald Silver Issue Editor

Donald Silver

Donald Silver  

Psychoanalytic investigations of the lives of prominent individuals—psychobiographies—are practically as old as psychoanalysis itself. Freud's classic study of Leonardo da Vinci of 1910 forms the prototype of an entire genre of “pathography” that blossomed in the decades to follow. Yet, such early efforts were both self-limited and self-limiting: they attempted to “reduce” creative achievements to the vicissitudes of psychosexual development, frequently falling prey to what Erikson would term “originology”—the attempt to reduce life to patterns of recurrence without understanding it as the organic compound of individual and social growth.

The essays in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry provide compelling testimony to the fact that recent advances in psychoanalytic theory have brought in their wake corresponding advances in the subtlety, scope, and persuasiveness of psychobiography. One might say that the creativity evinced by a recent generation of psychoanalytic theorists has rendered analysis better able to grasp a maximally creative individual like Goethe. In approaching Goethe's creative output, these studies far transcend the stereotypically “oedipal” approach of the first generation of pathographies. In line with recent theoretical advances, they look to preoedipal mother-infant relationship, early idealizing and mirroring relationships, pathological object relationships, and complex defensive operations in apprehending the products of creative genius.

Goethe has proven an ideal subject for exemplifying the most recent trends in psychobiography. His generous and revelatory correspondence, teamed with his remarkable autobiographical chronicle, Poetry and Truth, testify to his own recognition that creativity is always embedded in life history.

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

All our contributors approach the subject of the structural theory that evolved from the writings of Rapaport (1951), Hartmann (1950, 1953), and Hartmann, Kris, and Loewenstein (1949) with a degree of restlessness. Some contributors believe that the structural and tripartite theories should be substantially modified because they lack explanatory power for the analytic process. They believe theories based upon systems or schemata processing is better suited to explain the analytic situation. Others believe that the structural theory should remain intact, although greater clarity is required in conceptualizing the hierarchy of theoretical abstraction and the application of the metapsychological principles. Still others believe that the structural theory should be discarded and replaced by a theory emphasizing an experience or a phenomenological viewpoint. Finally, one contributor emphasizes that theory must include a model of the model-maker.

Several questions are raised and left unanswered. Should the structural theory remain the principal theory of psychoanalysis or should it be one of several theories because no theory is adequate to encompass all psychological functions? Although it is argreed that psychic conflict is fundamental to mental life, are the boundaries between id, ego, and superego the principal localities for conflict? Furthermore, is a closed causal system of natural science or a phenomenological system of humanities best suited to conceptualized psychic phenomena?

Although the contributors share the same methodology in acquiring empirical data through the psychoanalytic method, we are left with a variety of views and questions when they use their data in psychoanalytic theorizing.

Love Among the Signifiers

Emmett Wilson

Emmett Wilson

Canal Road R.D. 1, Box 262
Princeton, N.J. 08540

Emmett Wilson  

There are certainly more conventional approaches to psychoanalytic discussions in France than are represented by the articles in this issue. It seems to me that what the editors have tried to do, as far as possible, has been to maintain a theme of confrontation, after the name of the organization under whose auspices the exchange in Paris took place. The articles here show some of the differences in the intellectual approach of French psychoanalytic writers, so that for an American audience there is an intellectual confrontation with what is different and distinct in French psychoanalytic thought. With a range of topics so disparate as those in the articles presented here, it is impossible to give a systematic and thorough response. Because the articles show a special emphasis on language, it is primarily to language and to the signifier, this entity so strange perhaps to an American audience, that I shall direct my remarks. Even then I must be somewhat impressionistic and superficial, and there are many important issues that I cannot touch in the space available.

A few words are in order on the historical situation and new approach that characterizes the work of Confrontation. This group, founded in 1974 by René Major and the late Dominique Geahchan, has been of importance, I think, in contemporary French psychoanalysis. For all that its name might imply, this group has represented a synthetic or healing tendency which has developed of late in French psychoanalytic circles. Analysts, who once would have nothing to do with one another, now meet in Confrontation.

291

The Effect of Guilt Feelings on the Structuring of a Text: The Depiction of the Friederike Episode in Goethe's Autobiography

Martin Stern

Martin Stern

Clarastrasse 13
CH - 4058 Basel
Switzerland

Martin Stern  

With goethe we have before us a strange situation in which the most significant German autobiographer is also a decided opponent of every contemplative act that is directed solely at one's own self.1 Goethe writes about this aversion in an 1823 essay, in which he wanted to thank the natural scientist Heinroth for a sympathetic assessment of his (Goethe's) own scientific thought: “I hereby confess that that seemingly noble task “know thyself” has always sounded suspicious to me, like a ruse on the part of secretly allied priests, who wanted to confuse man with unattainable demands and to lead him astray, away from activity in the outer world to a false inner tranquility.

Professor Stern teaches German literature at the University of Basel, Switzerland.

A longer version of this article appeared in Stern, 1982.

1In accord with the current developments in research, the term autobiography will from now on refer to that particular integral form which is one's retrospective depiction of one's own self and one's experiences; it has emerged in German literature as a distinct form since the pietistic movement. Earlier forms tended toward being either “memoirs,” which were scarcely introspective but merely chronological reports, or “confessions,” which were self-analysis concentrating entirely on the observation of the soul. Aside from a few important exceptions such as Augustinus and Cardano, not until the eighteenth century was a tradition established that presented a point of view that integrated the self and the world.591

Why Goethe? Some Concluding Remarks in Summary

Helen Schoenhals MD

Helen Schoenhals

Westendstr. 92
6000 Frankfurt/Main
West Germany

Helen Schoenhals  

Why does a psychoanalytic journal devote an issue to the theme “Goethe”? Wurmser's interpretation of how Goethe's ideas have much in common with the way psychoanalysts think and how they do their work provides one answer to this question. Before the articles of this journal are reviewed, however, something should be said in general about what psychoanalysis has to do with literature and whether it is justified to use psychoanalytic theory in the interpretation of literary works.

Many literary critics today would cringe at the thought of applying psychoanalytic theory to works of art in order to understand the artist, his motivation, his creative process, or even to understand the art work itself, to the degree that biographical and historical material is used in order to do this. Beginning with the New Criticism at the turn of the century, literary works were to be appreciated and analyzed according to their characteristics as works of art and not according to their connections with the author. If an art work was really a work of art, it could and should stand alone. “Art for art's sake” became a cliché, as well as James Joyce's (1916, p. 215)

Dr. Schoenhals is a psychoanalyst and staff member in the Department of Psychotherapy and Psychosomatic Medicine at the J. W. Goethe University Hospital, Frankfurt, West Germany. She is originally from Detroit and has a Master's degree from the University of Michigan in comparative literature.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Warren Poland Issue Editor and René Major Issue Editor

René Major

René Major  

In the spring of 1983, a group of French and American analysts met in Paris to compare theories and clinical practices in the two countries. The question behind the meeting was captured in its working title: “Two Paths, One Goal?” This issue grew out of that meeting. The satisfaction of the participants in part revealed the anticipatory, cautious skepticism with which each group had approached the other. The Americans half-expected to find the French obscure and preoccupied with semiotics, detached from clinical experience. The French half-expected to find the Americans mechanistic and preoccupied with abstruse metapsychology. Instead, all discovered a common set of struggles in trying to grasp, describe, and understand clinical psychoanalytic experience.

Included in this issue are both French papers discussed at that meeting and others presented here in English for the first time. France is an intellectually vibrant country, bubbling with diversity. It would be as erroneous to view France from across the ocean as a stereotyped, monolithic caricature of Jacques Lacan as it would be to view us from that distance as a similarly sterotyped monolith modeled on a caricature of Heinz Hartmann or Heinz Kohut. These figures have been vital influences, the sources of contributions and controversies. But in neither country has analytic thought been narrowly limited to any one school.

The papers in this issue have been selected as a sampling of the range of ideas of French analytic thought. As a result, the contents are not exhaustive in their breadth, inevitably omitting other valued contributors. Limited by the space available, we have had to make a limited choice of papers. All of the authors are practicing clinical psychoanalysts; their backgrounds and their orientations vary.

Models as Vehicles of Transference: Observations from Biographical Studies

George Moraitis MD

George Moraitis

180 North Michigan Avenue
Chicago, Illinois 60601

George Moraitis  

The science of psychoanalysis has, from its discovery, utilized a variety of scientific models designed to guide the psychoanalytic investigator in the collection, classification, and interpretation of observations made. Models serve as provisional maps for those who travel into an uncharted territory. Although the reliability of these maps cannot be guaranteed, their usefulness is undeniable. Through the use of scientific models, perceptions are organized into coherent and communicable schemata about which some degree of consensus has been reached over a period of time. Despite the fact that there can be no certainty about the accuracy of scientific models, their use constitutes an effective way for the investigator to communicate his perceptions to others and facilitates the dialogue necessary for any intellectual pursuit.

In this paper I use the term model in a broad sense in an effort to by-pass complex issues of definition and distinction between it and such other related terms as schema, paradigm, or prototype. Although I am quite sure one can postulate several levels of distinction in the use and meaning of such terms, it is extremely difficult to reach a consensus about them.

Dr. Moraitis is a Supervising and Training Analyst with the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Almost 90 years have passed since the discovery of psychoanalysis as a treatment of mental illness. Yet the theory of psychoanalytic technique remains ambiguous and vulnerable. We are still searching for explanations of what characterizes the therapeutic role of the psychoanalyst. What are the components of the therapeutic intervention? How do we integrate an interactional, intersubjective, and intrapsychic point of view?

The commentaries in this issue on Gill's Analysis of Transference, Volume I and Gill and Hoffman's Analysis of Transference, Volume II (9 annotated audio-recorded sessions) focus directly on the fundamental technical principles of psychoanalysis. Because of the thoroughness and credibility of Gill's arguments, the reader is forced to review and reevaluate the usefulness of accepted clinical concepts and techniques. We share the reaction expressed in Sandler and Sandler's commentary: “…and even though many colleagues will to varying degrees have reservations about some of his propositions, we can expect that psychoanalytic theory of technique will never be the same again!”

Gill asserts that central to psychoanalysis is the analysis of the transference, defined as an inseparable component of all the interactions between analysand and analyst. This premise, in addition to a revised conception of resistance—resistance to the awareness of the transference and resistance of the resolution of the transference—presents a challenge to analysts of all schools of thought. What place should be assigned to extratransference interpretation and to genetic search and reconstruction? Does transference interpretation and the active pursuit of resistance to the awareness of transference receive insufficient attention in the technique of analysts in general?

Ernest Wolf MD

Ernest Wolf

180 North Michigan Avenue
Chicago, Illinois 60601

Ernest Wolf  

Nothing of him that doth fade,

But doth suffer a sea-change

Into something rich and strange.

— Tempest, I, ii, 397

Not since leo stone's The Psychoanalytic Situation (1963) has a book about psychoanalytic treatment caught my interest as much as Merton Gill's and Irwin Hoffman's Analysis of Transference (1982). Stone's slim volume was like a refreshing breeze of relaxed spontaneity wafting over the rigidly ruled technical percepts that had guided psychoanalytic treatment during the post-Freudian supremacy of Hartmann's ego psychology. Stone's opus was received with much skepticism and only gradually gained a wider hearing. But quiet waters run deep, and the appearance of Gill and Hoffman's monographs testifies to the sea change that is occurring in psychoanalysis and to which the Analysis of the Transference makes an important contribution.

Analysis of Transference is a bold yet carefully thought out, scholarly, and, on the whole, successful attempt to clarify our thinking about transference by a systematic reexamination of current usage in actual practice. Gill and Hoffman (1982), in a companion volume, illustrate the main issues by videotaped transcripts.

Gill finds the general technical quality of much psychoanalytic practice not to his taste.

Dr. Wolf is Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis.

Familiarity

Serge Viderman

Serge Viderman

15 rue des Beaux Arts
75006 Paris
France

Serge Viderman  

I used to like epigraphs. I like them less now, but something of the feeling remains. I would like to reproduce a painting of Magritte's here, the one showing a pipe with the inscription: “Ceci n'est pas un pipe” (“This is not a pipe”).

From one pipe to another, or from transference to a history.

Why do we always speak of transference love, never of transference hate? If transference were what it is alleged to be, both passions would be reproduced in it. There may be such a thing as transference love, but not transference hate. The analytic space would explode.

Transference love itself poses a formidable problem, which Freud saw — that of echte Liebe. But can echte Liebe and transference love be reconciled? It would be ridiculous for me to define echte Liebe. I have too many predecessors. What probably makes transference love viable in analysis, and analysis viable in transference, is that the analysand, whatever is wrong with him, as well as the analyst, whatever he pretends, both know they are acting. Except the psychotic. The consequences of this can be seen. What we are acting, on the other hand, every day, fortunately, is more Labiche than Racine.1

Originally published in French in Études Freudiennes, vol. 19/20 (1982), pp. 52-63. Saul Steinberg drawing reproduced by permission of the artist.

1Both were French playwrights — the former, a master of “Boulevard” comedy; the latter, of “classical” tragedy.151

Biographical Sketch: Merton M. Gill

Robert Holt PHD

Robert Holt

6 Washington Place
New York, New York 10003

Robert Holt  

Merton max gill was born in chicago on July 26, 1914. This special issue, occasioned primarily by the importance of his recent twin monograph on transference, thus happily affords his friends and colleagues the opportunity also to celebrate the 70th birthday of a man who is not only widely respected for his many scientific and professional contributions but is loved and cherished as a person.

When I first met Mert, about 38 years ago, only eight years had passed since he had received his MD (from the University of Chicago, where he also did his undergraduate work). After an internship at Michael Reese Hospital, he had finally made the break from Chicago to take a residency in psychiatry at the Menninger Clinic. By 1946, he had not only become a staff member but had been Chief of the Outpatient Department for a year and was freshly become Assistant Director of the Research Department, David Rapaport's right-hand man. A pretty rapid rise for a 32-year-old man. No one seemed to look on Mert as a “boy wonder,” however. He was mature for his years, and clearly possessed not only intellectual brilliance but a charismatic personal quality that has always drawn people to him. He completed his psychoanalytic training in the Topeka Institute in 1947.

Dr. Holt is Professor of Psychology at New York University, where he founded the Research Center for Mental Health and served as its Director until 1969. He is recipient of United States Public Health Service Research Career Award No. 5-K06-MH-12455, from the National Institute of Mental Health, which supported the preparation of this paper.

Goethe's Elective Affinities: Themes on Loss and Restoration

Jon Shaw MD

Jon Shaw

5225 Connecticut Avenue
Washington, D.C. 20015

Jon Shaw  

Elective affinities published in 1809 is one of the least well-known and perhaps least valued contributions in Goethe's literary heritage. It seems, nevertheless, to have been of great personal significance to the aging Goethe. Speaking of the novel, Goethe stated, “No one can fail to recognize in it a deep passionate wound which shrinks from being closed by healing, a heart which dreads to be cured…. In it, as in a burial urn, I have deposited with deep emotion many a sad experience. … the feelings it embodies can never quite depart from me” (Lewes, 1855, p. 318). What is the nature of the “deep passionate wound” which shrinks from being healed and the “heart which dreads to be cured”? Certainly his words suggest a man mourning a loss, yet unable or perhaps unwilling to sever the attachment.

It is my belief that the meaning of the paradoxical existence of a deep passionate wound associated with a great suffering that yet dreads to be healed this paradox reflects the dialectical nature of creativity in relation to the mourning process.

Dr. Shaw is Psychiatry and Neurology Consultant, Office of the Surgeon General, Pentagon, Washington, D.C.; Professor of Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, Bethesda, Maryland. He is also Clinical Associate Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Georgetown University Medical School, Washington, D.C.

Robert Langs MD

Robert Langs

30 East 60th Street

Robert Langs  

It is my considered opinion that Merton Gill, with the assistance of Irwin Hoffman, has made a significant contribution to the clinical theory and practice of psychoanalysis and psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy. This statement is based not only on the convincing theoretical arguments presented by Gill in volume one (1982) and the perceptive analysis of clinical material offered by Gill and Hoffman (1982) in the second volume of this work, but also on my own 15 years of clinical research, deeply empirical in nature, which has led to the development of the communicative approach to classical psychoanalysis (see especially Langs, 1982). In many critical ways, the clinical findings and theoretical conclusions of Gill and Hoffman correspond strongly with the results of my own clinical investigations — a point alluded to briefly in the first volume of the present work. These studies lend extensive and independent support to many of the ideas presented by Gill and Hoffman.

My own views on virtually every issue discussed by Gill are available in my writings (see especially Langs, 1972, 1975, 1976a, b, c, 1978a, b, c, 1979, 1980, 1981a, b, 1982).

Being Alone with One's Mother: The Horror of Incest

Conrad Stein

Conrad Stein

4, villa d'Eylau
75116, Paris
France

Conrad Stein  

The following pages from L'Enfant imaginaire are a translation of the bulk of Chapter 7, entitled “L'Horreur de l'inceste,” and two short fragments from Chapter 8, entitled “Le Désir incestueux.”1 They seemed to me sufficiently autonomous to satisfy the requirements of an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry devoted to the clinical work of French analysts.

To tell the truth, for some time now I have failed to see any merit in the traditional distinction between clinical and theoretical work in the field of psychoanalysis. With the introductory and concluding episodes here set aside,2 my study concerns three consecutive sessions with the same patient. As such, it might be characterized as “clinical.” But in what does it consist, if not an elaboration of interpretations? Interpretations initially of particular application, which emerged either in the sessions themselves or after the event in the process of writing and on the basis of which I have risked what Habermas has called “general interpretations.” If it is true that to interpret is to theorize and that interpretation is the only mode of theorizing specific to psychoanalytic thinking, then this study would earn the characterization “theoretical.”

Translated by J. G. May.

1See Stein's L'Enfant Imaginaire (1971, pp. 120-133, 141-143, 151-152). Also translated in Italian as L'Immaginario: Strutture Psichoanalitiche (Milan: Feltrinelli, 1972), and into Spanish as El Niño imaginario (Barcelona: Martinez Roca, 1977).2The introductory episode was reconsidered in my book Aussi je vous aime bien (1978, pp. 15-27). There I discuss the extent to which this exchange between a patient and his psychoanalyst concerned me personally.269

I am convinced that a psychoanalytic study, even when it is not explicitly cast in a literary style reflecting the fact, is efficacious only to the extent that it evinces something of the work of interpretation. Taken as a whole, Freud's oeuvre is, in my opinion, of just this sort. I am equally convinced that the body of general interpretations left us by Freud — those comprising what is usually and unhappily called Freudian theory (thus permitting the view that they constitute a causally governed system) — is inapplicable as a resource for guiding one's practice. If knowledge of this corpus is indispensable, it is only because the work of interpretation in particular cases rests on its recurrence in the form of reminiscences. In other words, with respect at least to the essentials, it seems to me that a psychoanalyst can only rediscover for his own purposes what Freud discovered before him, that his route can consist only in retracing that of Freud.3 The reader should not be surprised, therefore, to find here a fragment that awakens in him Freudian reminiscences, enough so that, notwithstanding the fact that only the most casual reference is made to Freud's texts, he shall recognize it without difficulty as a Freudian labor.

Shortly after being named to the Teaching Commission of the Institut de Psychanalyse in Paris, I suddenly realized, confronted with the necessity of accounting for the fact that my patients' sessions with me permitted them to progress in their analyses, that everything I had learned as a student was worth scarcely more that the explanations given by Sganarelle in Molière's Le Médecin malgré lui that ended in the celebrated line: “This is the reason why your daughter is mute.” L'Enfant imaginaire, a study of the psychoanalytic process, is the result of this crisis. Old slates had to be wiped clean and a fresh start made from scratch; and through this effort I came to understand that, while deliberate references were sterile, reminiscences proved themselves fruitful.

3In this regard, see “Une Conférence sur l'identification à Freud,” Chapter IV of my collection of articles from 1959 to 1972, entitled La Mort d'Oedipe (1977, pp. 75-91). The book has been translated into Italian as La Morte de Edipo (Milan: Spirali Editioni, 1983), and into Spanish as La Muerte de Edipo (Buenos Aires: Neuva Visión, 1978).270

Wanting to submit Freud's statements to evaluation by confronting them with new experience is just as vain as regarding them as directly applicable to one's practice. In such matters, one must break with traditional views all the more entrenched because initiated by Freud himself, but nevertheless contrary to the real genuis of the discipline Freud promoted. It makes no more sense to seek to understand Freud's works in terms of their truth or falsity, their validity or superannuation, than it does to impose these categories on Shakespeare's plays. Precisely because of his concern to demonstrate and to enlist the support of reason, Freud's oeuvre is teeming with pitfalls, oddities, logical difficulties, and contradictions; the effects of truth can emerge only from a reading that interprets all these pecularities from the point of view of their necessity and, in this way, accounts for their genesis. The commentary so conceived is not the only evidence of the fecundity of the reading, however. Following the critical work that comprises the commentary, the text returns on the sly in the subsequent work of the reader.

In this respect, revising the following pages for translation held some surprises in store for me. Apart from a brief notice in his Draft N of May 31, 1897, Freud seems to have mentioned the horror of incest only in Totem and Taboo and in a few subsequent passages having reference to this book. Why would I have thought of Freud's “attempt at applying the point of view and the findings of psycho-analysis to some unsolved problems of social psychology” (1913, p. xiii) while I was studying three sessions with a patient? Indeed, I don't remember having thought of it. A few years before, however, I'd devoted a rather long study to Totem and Taboo. There, I had tried to highlight the interpretation of mother-in-law taboo that crowns the book's first chapter, “The Horror of Incest,” and to show that this interpretation, although inapposite as formulated from the viewpoint of contemporary social anthropology is, nonetheless, inspired in another respect. I had further emphasized the fact that the book departs from the horror of incest to arrive at the murder of the father and ambivalence toward him. As I look back on it now, the step I took in writing what follows seems in certain

271

respects similar to the one taken by Freud. In addition, I was unaware that in affirming that it is not for fear of punishment by the law that men generally abstain from having sexual relations with their mothers, I was urging the exact contrary of one of Frazer's theses to which Freud had attached great importance (1913, p. 123). The relevation of these facts, the product of cryptomnesia, has opened new perspectives for me on an entire series of Freud's texts. I will have to resume their commentary.

To avoid any misunderstanding, I should point out that, again drawing on Freud in Totem and Taboo, I here employ the term “incest” exclusively to designate sexual relations between a son and his mother.

Nathalie Zaltzman  

Sexual [genital] love afforded him [man] the strongest experiences of satisfaction, and in fact provided him with the prototype of all happiness.

— Sigmund Freud, Civilization and Its Discontents

I. The Ambitions of Analytic Practice

In the beginning, the dazzling, naive promise of a unique kind of discipline and practice. If psychoanalysis is that set of conceptual and methodological means able to penetrate the forms and laws of the unconscious as they rule over each individual destiny, what other practice has a field of study as provocative as that of unconscious sexuality?

What other practice has the mission of serving phenomena so strange that they obey a principle known in its economic aim as the pleasure principle?

A predestined pact between a method and its object — to put Eros into words.

The encounter between an instinct pushing ceaselessly on toward its pleasure objectives and an experimental protocol designed specifically to reveal and produce the psychic incarnation of that instinctual energy — this working alliance legitimized all ambitions.

Although the psychoanalytic process has been discussed extensively in the psychoanalytic literature, these writings have usually been within the framework of standard psychoanalytic theory. Here we wish to examine the developmental processes of psychoanalytic treatment from the standpoint of a conceptual framework of information processing and systems theory, which we believe involves not merely a terminologic change but a significant conceptual change with wide-ranging implications.

We use the term developmental processes here in the broad sense to refer to those progressive and relatively orderly changes in complexity of psychological organization and function that occur in the course of a psychoanalysis — changes in the patient, in the analyst, and in the analytic system itself. Although these changes are similar to those that normally transpire during growth and development, there are also differences. In child development, if the environment cannot respond appropriately to the child's maturational attainments, deficiencies occur, in addition to distortions that occur on the basis of conflict. But the developmental processess of treatment (of whatever kind) cannot resupply the maturational epoch which has been passed.

I am of course grateful to my critics1 for the attention they have given my work and for the generally friendly tone of their comments even when they have important objections to make. My rejoinder is essentially organized around two main points. First, I both accept and reject, as I shall be explaining in detail, the justice of the criticism that I have overemphasized the centrality of the analysis of the transference. Second, the monograph fails to make clear my espousal of a minority conceptualization of transference which differs significantly from the generally accepted one, in that, as Hoffman (1983) puts it, the minority view conceptualizes transference in a social as against an asocial paradigm. Though I later discuss that changed conception of transference in detail, I summarize it here as a rejection of the view that there is a dichotomy between transference and nontransference and that that dichotomy is between the distorted and the realistic.

There is a connection between the criticism and the failure, in that had I been clearer in my own mind about the changed conception of transference, I would have been more enthusiastic about the contribution I was making in that regard and somewhat less focused on the centrality issue. My personal tendency to hyperbole also played a role.

The Fate of the Five Metapsychological Principles

Howard Shevrin PHD

Howard Shevrin

Riverview Building — 900 Wall Street
Ann Arbor, Michigan 48105

Howard Shevrin  

The five metapsychological principles set forth by Rapaport and Gill in 1959 have flown like regimental colors above psychoanalysis. But the ranks of marchers following behind are rapidly depleting. One general is dead and the other has marched off in another direction under different banners; and some of the once loyal troops are shooting at the colors, leaving several in tatters. The metapsychological enterprise itself is accused of being a snare and a delusion — an empty, abstract neurologizing of psychoanalysis which is in accord with neither clinical observations nor contemporary neurology. Are we in danger of being left with these few tattered banners and no army, no generals, and no cause?

It will be my purpose in this paper to show that some psychoanalytic theoreticians who are urging us to abandon metapsychology may be leading us away from clinical reality even as they profess to draw us closer. I am referring in particular to the contributions of Gill (1976), Klein (1976), Holt (1976), and Schafer (1975). My main contention will be that much recent theorizing has failed because several significant distinctions have either been ignored or obliterated. The distinctions I have in mind are those that enable us to set apart from each other considerations of method, technique, and theory. Of necessity, these issues are complex, abstract, yet necessary for informed clinical practice and its scientific investigation.

Dr. Shevrin is Professor of Psychology in the Departments of Psychiatry and Psychology, and Director of the Psychotherapy Evaluation and Treatment Laboratory, University of Michigan.

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Do psychoanalysts need models? The answer to this question was a self-evident “YES!” when Freud proposed his models of the mind in successive stages and revisions. Each model provided the growing psychoanalytic movement with a powerful tool with which to assimilate the data pouring in from new discoveries. But more than that, Freud's models ensured the expanding field with unifying concepts — hypothetical diagrams that all analysts could share and add to. Yet there has always been some undercurrent of dissent. Many analysts were loath to replace the topographic model with the structural one. Others have felt put off by Freud's philosophic speculations — seeing in models the witch metapsychology who would distract the clinician from his task of treating patients. Once the relative unity of the early period dissolved, models came under increasing question, should they be experience-near or more abstract and therefore more encompassing? In what language should they be expressed?

While it is possible to be troubled by such controversy, our view is that it represents a degree of success of the model-makers of the past. The more precise and refined a model becomes, the more its shortcomings can be appreciated. Although Freud was always somewhat fuzzy at the edges in his models, narrower focusing by later analysts from differing schools has exposed the limitations of both the old and newer models.

In this issue on psychoanalytic models we present two facets of the subject: new models that current analysts believe will best serve our theory and practice; and critiques or defenses of older models. As the reader will see, each paper represents both a proposed point of view and a direct or implicit critique of other proposals.

The interface between the empirical base of psychoanalysis and its theoretical concepts has been an area for unending discussion, dispute, and debate. An extensive literature has developed dealing with questions regarding the manner in which psychoanalytic theory is generated on the basis of empirical clinical data, on the validity of such theoretical formulations, and particularly on issues related to problems of vertification (Sherwood, 1969; Eagle, 1973; Rubinstein, 1975; Thomae & Kaechele, 1975).

The same interface gives rise to a different set of problems when viewed in the perspective of the influence of theory on the clinical process. Puzzling questions arise that are difficult to resolve. Does theory make a difference in the clinical situation? If so, how? In what ways do theoretical formulations and understandings enter into and shape the clinical process? Does the whole of the theory make a difference or only some parts of it? What kind of theory might make such a difference? Does metapsychology make a real difference? And if so, how?

One particular current of recent psychoanalytic thinking has brought these issues into more dramatic focus. I refer to the radical criticism of psychoanalytic metapsychology and its related scientific methodology.

This paper presents an overview of our efforts to rethink the conceptual and methodological foundations of psychoanalysis. These efforts have been guided by three general considerations. First, we have felt that any new framework should be capable of preserving the contributions made by the classical analytic theorists and of translating these contributions into a common conceptual language. Second, it is our view that the theory of psychoanalysis should be formulated on an experience-near level of discourse, closely anchored in the phenomena of clinical observation. The third guiding consideration is found in our belief that an adequate theory of personality should illuminate the structure, significance, origins, and therapeutic transformations of personal subjective worlds in all their richness and diversity.

It has been merton gill's fate to be an acknowledged leader in (American) psychoanalysis almost from the beginning of his career. An uncommon percentage of his writings have been almost instantly — and justly — hailed for their critical influence at particular points in the history of analysis in America, in relation both to psychoanalytic clinical practice (and its relation to the derivative dynamic psychotherapies) and to psychoanalytic theory formulation (in the ascendency and then the decline of ego psychology — the apotheosis of metapsychology). Witness the 1954 paper, “Psychoanalysis and Exploratory Psychotherapy,” which (together with Edward Bibring's essay of the same year) more than any other contributions from the various panels and symposia of 1952-1954 set our understanding of the nature of psychoanalysis as a therapy, in all its similarities to and differences from the congeries of dynamic psychotherapies elaborated within its framework. Or consider the 1959 paper co-authored with David Rapaport, “The Points of View and Assumptions of Metapsychology,” which so concisely defined and capped the full elaboration of the metapsychological points of view including the co-equal placement among them of the adaptive point of view.

Nobody—Anybody—Somebody

François Roustang

François Roustang

96 rue Miromesnil
75008 Paris
France

François Roustang  

One day in the year 1892, the patient he had just cured threw her arms around his neck. He told himself what he had suspected for some time: “That gesture cannot be the result of my charms. It was not intended for me.” This suspicion gave birth to the idea of transference, that “false connection” as Freud first called it with unmatched precision. Transference is thus a love letter without an address, the result of an omission: the psychotherapist withdraws as an individual in order to allow himself to take the place of her other, her indissociable other whom she loves today, whom she may detest tomorrow. Transference therefore is love addressed to nobody, for it is addressed to her other, a protean, unstable yet imperious image.

This other that I am is the product of the meeting and interpenetration of images, people, events, or things with which I have identified, wanted to identify, or could not help myself from being identified with. In short this other is the product of all the landmarks in my life, whether I am aware of them or not, of all the characteristics which have blended into a new me, inevitably different from the other individuals of my species. But these more or less unified images, simultaneously faces, figures, accidents, or objects, are not merely the history of my distinctiveness.

Originally published in French in Études Freudiennes, vol. 19/20 (1982), pp. 27-33.

Transference Analysis: Means or End?

Arnold Richards MD

Arnold Richards

40 East 89th Street
New York, New York 10128

Arnold Richards  

Over the years psychoanalysts have invoked different organizing frameworks as vehicles for theoretical and clinical discourse. The concept of “identity” was a prominent theme in the 1960s, to be supplanted by a focus on the “self” in the 1970s. Now, in the 1980s, preoccupation with the self and its vicissitudes is giving way to a revived interest in the psychoanalytic process per se. In part the result of a growing disillusionment with proliferating alternative theories, this renewed interest may have been kindled as well by the debate over Kohut's “self psychology” and its attentiveness to the role of empathy in the analytic transaction. Schafer's The Analytic Attitude (1983) and Anton Kris's Free Association: Method and Process (1983) exemplify this new focus on the psychoanalytic process. It is in this emerging tradition that Merton Gill's two-volume study, The Analysis of the Transference (Gill, 1982; Gill & Hoffman, 1982) must be situated as well. Like Schafer and Kris, Gill seeks to explicate the methods and goals of psychoanalysis by concentrating on a particular dimension of the analytic process. What narrative content is to Shafer and free association is to Kris, the analysis of transference is to Gill.

Gill's position is informed by the conviction that the analysis of the transference, which he considers “the heart of psychoanalytic technique,” has not been consistently pursued in practice.

Dr. Richards is Assistant Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the New York University Medical Center and on the faculty of the Psychoanalytic Institute at New York University Medical Center.

In spite of Franco-American exchanges over the last few years, psychoanalytic research in either language remains relatively little known to the other. This is not due merely to lack of information but also to a disparity at times in how analysis is practiced and views its objectives. The question of how goethe has influenced freud personally has been addressed by most writers on Freud's life and the early history of psychoanalysis. Yet how relevant some of Goethe's central philosophical tenets may have been for the scientific method chosen by Freud for psychoanalysis has, as far as I am aware of, not been raised. I believe that in the current debate about the true nature of psychoanalysis (psychoanalysis as natural science? as hermeneutics? as science of self-reflection? as art? as mythology? as separate field of symbolic forms?) the following considerations may have some value.

“Do not the most beautiful colors of life appear to us only against a dark foil?” Thus begins the seventh book of Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship. And elsewhere Goethe wrote: “A tender poem, like a rainbow, is drawn only on a dark background; therefore the element of depression fits the poetic genius.”1

Dr. Wurmser is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the University of West Virginia.

Goethe: Sibling Rivalry and Faust

Charles Kligerman MD

Charles Kligerman

180 North Michigan Avenue
Chicago, Illinois 60601.

Charles Kligerman  

In the following presentation I wish to call attention to the special role that conflicts over sibling rivalry played as a lifelong motivating factor in the psyche of Goethe and as a central theme in his masterwork Faust. It goes without saying that a universal genius like Goethe, with the incredible richness of both his personality and his multifaceted creativity, would defy adequate explanation even by the most thorough research and the most sensitive psychoanalytic understanding. Eissler emphasizes this point in the introduction to his own monumental study of Goethe (1963), a work that actually makes giant strides toward that ideal.

Similarly, a work like Faust, the writing of which spanned the major portion of the poet's existence, is intensely autobiographical, as was everything Goethe wrote. The final version contained so much of the accumulated philosophy and wisdom of his long and fruitful life that it obviously could not be reduced to a single theme. Yet, the greatest and most complicated of men can be driven in the unconscious by strikingly few crucial issues, and I believe the sibling rivalry problem to be one such decisive issue in Goethe.

Dr. Kligerman is a Training Analyst and member of the faculty at the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis.

Goethe and His Sister: Some Literary Vicissitudes of a Relationship

James Read MD

James Read

800 Pershing Drive
Silver Spring, Maryland 20910

James Read  

The relationship between goethe and his sister, Cornelia, has been referred to by students of his life as somewhat strangely close or unusually intimate. Both Brion (1982) and Freidenthal (1965) refer to Goethe's tendency to seek out “sisters” in his love relationships. The tie between the two has figured as an essential component in a pathography by Theilhaber (1929). Eissler (1963) in his insightful study gives the relationship a central and balanced place. My own focus will be principally on some literary vicissitudes of the relationship, which emphasize what I consider an important leitmotiv for Goethe — the ideal and idealized woman who exerts a beneficial and ennobling influence on the man and who can then redeem him, and its counterpart, the woman as desirable and yearned for, yet through her passivity or blindness ultimately giving only illusory encouragement and, in the end, unable to save the man from disaster.

First, we should note some burdens for the English-speaking reader in evaluating Goethe's vast literary output. We are outside the German cultural orbit. His works are often difficult to obtain in translation, and his magnificent gifts of eloquence — particularly in the lyric poetry — are not easily translatable.

Dr. Read is Assistant Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at George Washington University School of Medicine; he is on the faculty of the Baltimore-D.C. Institute for Psychoanalysis.
